questions.stem: The influenza PCR is pending. For each safety measure, indicate whether it is indicated or contraindicated now.

rows.text: Droplet precautions until the influenza result is back
A low bed with the bed alarm on
Soft wrist restraints to stop the client pulling at the oxygen
Head of the bed at 30 degrees or more during care and meals

questions.educationalObjective: Generate safety and infection-control measures for a confused client with pneumonia.

exhibits.title: Admission orders, 0930
exhibits.body: Influenza and COVID-19 PCR sent. Admit to ICU. Fall precautions. The client has pulled at the nasal cannula twice.

questions.stem: Review the 0945 data. Which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.

options.text: Draw blood cultures from two sites before the first antibiotic
Give the ceftriaxone within the first hour
Hold the azithromycin and tell the provider the QTc
Titrate oxygen to an SpO2 of 92% to 96%
Wait for the sputum culture before starting antibiotics

rationale.correct: In severe pneumonia with sepsis: cultures, then antibiotics within the hour, oxygen to target, and a check for drug interactions and unsafe drugs before giving them.

perOption.a: Cultures first, so the organism can be found, without delaying antibiotics past the first hour.
perOption.b: Early antibiotics lower deaths in sepsis.
perOption.c: Azithromycin and citalopram both prolong the QT; with a QTc of 510 ms, another drug such as doxycycline is safer.
perOption.e: Metformin is held in sepsis with hypoperfusion and a raised lactate because of lactic acidosis risk.

questions.stem: Highlight the findings that show a life-threatening asthma attack.

segments.text: was intubated for asthma 2 years ago
speaks 2 or 3 words at a time
uses the neck muscles to breathe
faint wheezes with poor air movement

rationale.correct: Heavy rescue use, prior intubation, words-only speech, accessory muscles and a quiet chest mark a life-threatening attack.

perOption.s2: Heavy rescue use shows the attack is not responding.
perOption.s4: Prior intubation is the strongest risk factor for fatal asthma.
perOption.s6: Being unable to speak in sentences shows severe airflow limitation.
perOption.s8: Accessory muscle use shows a severe attack.
perOption.s10: Less wheezing with poor air movement means very little air is moving.
perOption.s12: Age is not a severity marker here.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize cues of severe asthma.

questions.stem: For each finding, choose the best interpretation.

cells.text: ABG at 2200: pH 7.47, PaCO2 32 mm Hg
ABG at 2245: pH 7.33, PaCO2 48 mm Hg
A systolic fall of 20 mm Hg on inspiration

options.text: Respiratory alkalosis from hyperventilation, expected early in an attack
Respiratory acidosis from tiring respiratory muscles
Improvement, because the pH is closer to normal
Pulsus paradoxus from severe air trapping

rationale.correct: A PaCO2 that rises from low to normal or high during a severe attack means exhaustion, not recovery.

perOption.b1:a: Early in asthma, fast breathing blows off CO2.
perOption.b1:d: The pH and PaCO2 are both abnormal.
perOption.b2:a: A rising PaCO2 in a severe attack means the client can no longer move enough air.
perOption.b2:b: The pH has passed normal into acidosis.
perOption.b2:c: HCO3- is normal and PaCO2 is high.
perOption.b3:a: Large pressure swings in the chest with severe obstruction.
perOption.b3:b: Possible in other settings; here it reflects air trapping.
perOption.b3:c: Not the cause in this picture.

exhibits.title: Prescriptions, 2250
exhibits.body: Albuterol 10 mg/hour continuous nebulizer. Ipratropium 0.5 mg nebulized every 20 minutes x3. Methylprednisolone 125 mg IV. Magnesium sulfate 2 g IV over 20 minutes. Lorazepam 1 mg IV as needed for anxiety. Propranolol 10 mg PO. Salmeterol 1 puff as needed.

questions.stem: Review the 2315 findings. Which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.

options.text: Call the rapid response or airway team now
Stay with the client and keep the head of the bed high
Give 100% oxygen by non-rebreather while the team comes
Prepare the intubation drugs and equipment
Leave to collect supplies from the stockroom
Give the lorazepam now to calm the client
Switch to a nasal cannula for comfort

rationale.correct: Impending respiratory arrest: get the airway team, stay, oxygenate, keep upright and prepare to intubate.

perOption.a: Worsening CO2 retention and drowsiness need airway experts.
perOption.b: Upright posture helps breathing; the client must not be left.
perOption.e: A deteriorating client is never left alone.

questions.educationalObjective: Generate the monitoring plan for TB drugs.

exhibits.title: Prescriptions
exhibits.body: Isoniazid 300 mg, rifampin 600 mg, pyrazinamide 1,500 mg and ethambutol 1,200 mg daily, with pyridoxine 25 mg daily. Directly observed therapy.

questions.stem: Which instructions should the nurse include in the client's teaching? Select all that apply.

options.text: Take the medicines every day for at least 6 months, even after feeling better
Use a barrier or other nonhormonal method of contraception
Expect orange urine, sweat and tears
Wear glasses rather than soft contact lenses
Stop the medicines if the urine turns orange
Return to work as soon as the cough settles

rationale.correct: Teaching covers finishing therapy, rifampin's effects on fluids, lenses and contraception, avoiding alcohol and when it is safe to return to work.

perOption.a: Stopping early leads to relapse and drug resistance.
perOption.d: Rifampin can permanently stain soft lenses.
perOption.g: The client returns to work only when no longer infectious, usually after 3 negative smears.

caseStudies.title: Severe community-acquired pneumonia in an older adult

exhibits.title: Emergency department, 0900
exhibits.body: An 82-year-old client is brought in by a daughter, who says the client has been "not making sense" since last night and has had a cough with rust-colored sputum for 3 days. The client lives alone and takes citalopram 20 mg daily, lisinopril 10 mg daily and metformin. Crackles and bronchial breath sounds over the right lower lobe. Oriented to person only. Chest x-ray: right lower lobe consolidation.

exhibits.title: Emergency department, 2200
exhibits.body: A 24-year-old client with asthma has been short of breath for 2 days and used an albuterol inhaler "every hour or so" today. The client was intubated for asthma 2 years ago and takes no controller medicine. The client sits forward with hands on the knees, speaks 2 or 3 words at a time, and uses the neck muscles to breathe. Faint wheezes are heard, with poor air movement at both bases. The systolic pressure falls 20 mm Hg on inspiration. Peak flow is 30% of the client's best.

caseStudies.title: COPD with CO2 narcosis from too much oxygen

exhibits.title: Medical unit, 0400
exhibits.body: A 68-year-old client with severe COPD, on 2 L/min home oxygen, was admitted yesterday with an exacerbation and green sputum. At 0200 the client said they were "short of breath", and the unlicensed assistive personnel (UAP) turned the oxygen up to 6 L/min by nasal cannula. At 0400 the client is hard to wake and mumbles. Skin is warm and flushed. Prescribed oxygen: titrate to SpO2 88% to 92%.

exhibits.title: Arterial blood gases and vital signs
Clinic, then admission
exhibits.body: A 45-year-old client who works at a homeless shelter has had a cough for 5 weeks, with blood-streaked sputum, night sweats and a 6 kg weight loss. The client lives with a partner and two school-age children. The client uses oral contraceptives and wears soft contact lenses. Chest x-ray: a cavity in the right upper lobe.
